Abstract
Knowledge graph completion (KGC) is used to infer new facts from existing facts. Embedding-based KGC methods efﬁciently
predict new facts by computing similarities among embeddings, whereas rule-based KGC methods achieve accuracy by
applying logical rules. Both methods are combined in studies that involve evaluating rules on the basis of the matching degree
between relation embeddings and scoring functions and using triplets derived from high-quality rules to enhance embedding
learning. Despite notable improvements, these rule evaluation methods are limited to simple models, and potential noise in
high-quality rules is frequently overlooked. To overcome these limitations, we propose the NAAER framework, a noise-aware
and model-agnostic framework that iteratively reﬁnes embeddings and rules. Our key innovation lies in the implementation
of a generalizable rule quality assessment that is conducted by measuring the absolute difference between the scores of the
rule body and the head triplets, coupled with adaptive noise reduction that is achieved via performance-guided rule ﬁltering.
Improvements in the link prediction performance of the NAAER framework were demonstrated using standard and sparse
datasets, illustrating the broad applicability of the rule evaluation method.
Keywords Knowledge graph completion · Knowledge graph embedding · Rule evaluation · Noise ﬁltering · Iterative learning

triplets are added to the knowledge graph to further enhance

2 Related works
2.1 Knowledge graph embeddings
Knowledge graph embedding (KGE) learns continuous vec-
tor representations for entities and relations. These low-
dimensional embeddings facilitate probabilistic assessment
of triplet plausibility through predeﬁned scoring functions.
Existing KGE methodos predominantly fall into three cate-
gories: (i) translation-based models (ii) semantic matching
models and (iii) neural network-based models.
Translation-based models represent relations as geometric
transformations in the embedding space. TransE (Bordes
et al. 2013) establishes a fundamental framework where, for
a given triplet (es,r, eo), the relation vector r operates as
a translation operator such that es + r ≈eo holds in ideal
cases. Although architecturally simple, TransE demonstrates
remarkable capability in modeling basic relational patterns,
which has led to its widespread adoption as a standard base-
line. RotatE (Sun et al. 2019) introduces a more sophisticated
paradigm by representing relations as rotations in complex
vector space, effectively capturing various relation patterns
such as symmetry, inverse, and composition.
Semantic matching-based models score triplets based on
the latent semantic similarity between entities and relations.
The foundational RESCAL framework (Nickel et al. 2011)
projects entities into vector spaces while modeling relations
as full-rank matrices. While relation matrices can model pair-
wise entity interactions, the O(d2) parameter complexity per
relation can led to overﬁtting. DistMult (Yang et al. 2015)
simpliﬁes RESCAL by imposing a diagonal constraint on
relation matrices. ComplEx (Trouillon et al. 2016) extends
DistMult into complex space and introduces the conjugate
transpose to handle asymmetry relations. Tucker (Balaževi´c
et al. 2019) factorizes a tensor into a core tensor multiplied
by matrices along each mode, allowing it to better capture
interactions between entities and relations.
Neural network-based models leverage deep learning archi-
tectures to model complex interactions between entities and
relations.ConvE(Dettmersetal.2018)pioneerstheuseof2D
convolutional ﬁlters to capture localized interaction patterns
between entity and relation embeddings through a reshap-
ing operation. MLI (Wang et al. 2023a) integrates recurrent
neural networks with factorized bilinear transformations to
simultaneously model both ﬁne-grained pairwise interac-
tions and coarse-grained relational semantics. MEGA (Wang
et al. 2023b) uniﬁes single-relation prediction with meta-
graph reasoning, thereby capturing both local and global
knowledge graph structures. RAGAT (Liu et al. 2021)
introduces a graph attention network as an encoder and Inter-
actE (Vashishth et al. 2020) as a decoder, fully considering
the graph structure of the knowledge graph and the impor-
tance of neighboring nodes.
2.2 Rule mining
Rule mining focuses on discovering logical rules from
observed data. AMIE (Galárraga et al. 2013) introduces
the partial completeness assumption (PCA) and PCA con-
ﬁdence to extract suitable rules from incomplete KGs. It
employs language biases, ensuring all variables in a rule
are closed or every atom is transitively connected, to reduce
the search space and enhance rule mining efﬁciency. Scal-
ability challenges are addressed by AnyBURL (Meilicke
et al. 2019), which employs an anytime bottom-up strategy.
This method generalizes speciﬁc triplets into probabilistic
rules through iterative reﬁnement, achieving computational
efﬁciency while maintaining interpretability. For complex
data dependencies, MICAR (Liu et al. 2022) introduces a
maximal information coefﬁcient framework, enabling the
extraction of nonlinear association rules (both positive and
negative forms) via a three-phase pipeline: data prepro-
cessing, candidate itemset generation, and rule induction.
SARM (Datta and Mali 2022) integrates multiple minimum
supports (MMS) with an efﬁcient correlation framework
(ECF), leveraging the downward closure property to prune
redundant itemsets. EduCe (Xu et al. 2023) enhances rule
diversity through dynamic weight mechanisms and constant
operators, enabling context-aware constant selection during
mining. FL-APOSD (Pang et al. 2023) models fuzzy linguis-
tic relationships via association nodes/paths, extracting non-
redundant rules while identifying maximal frequent attribute

2.3 Hybrid models
Hybrid models integrate embedding-based and rule-based
approaches to enhance knowledge graph completion, enforc-
ing compatibility between learned embeddings, observed
facts, and logical rules. These models typically operate
through iterative reﬁnement cycles that mutually reinforce
rule learning and representation learning.
KALE (Guo et al. 2016) establishes a t-norm fuzzy logic
framework where triplets are treated as atomic propositions.
The model computes composite rule truth values through
logical connectives and employs contrastive learning with
margin-based ranking to distinguish valid rules from con-
structednegatives.RUGE(Guoetal.2018)introducesadual-
consistency paradigm that aligns (i) embedding-generated
triplet scores with (ii) rule-derived conﬁdence estimates
through iterative mutual reﬁnement. RLvLR (Omran et al.
2019) pioneers path-based rule discovery, where relation
pathsarerepresentedasembeddingcompositions.Themodel
identiﬁes valid rules when path embeddings satisfy similar-
ity thresholds with target relations. DRUM (Sadeghian et al.
2019) advances this through neural tensor learning, com-
bining bidirectional RNNs for rule conﬁdence estimation
with low-rank tensor factorization for embedding reﬁne-
ment. IterE (Zhang et al. 2019) consists of three components:
embedding learning, axiom induction, and axiom injection.
Embedding learning utilizes existing methods to learn vec-
tor representations of entities and relations. Axiom induction
selects high-quality rules with scores exceeding the given
threshold. Axiom injection generates sparse entity triplets to
enhance the existing knowledge graph. Melo (Wang et al.
2023) incorporates entity meta-information into the IterE
framework to further boost the model’s link predictive per-
formance.
Beyond link prediction, the integration of symbolic rules
and KG embeddings has shown potential across various
downstream tasks. For instance: In question answering,
MKBQA (Wang et al. 2023) designs a series of logic rules
to convert natural language into triplets of the question and
employs a SimCSE-based similarity method to perform ﬁne-
grained alignment between the question triplet and potential
knowledge graph triplets. These technologies make MKBQA
can answer both computer science-related questions and
open domain questions. For recommendation, Spillo et al.
(2024) fuse rule-mined background knowledge with KG
triplet embeddings, simultaneously improving the predictive
accuracy and the novelty of the recommendations. In entity
alignment, PCE-HGTRA (Li et al. 2023) enhances entity
alignment by: (1) increasing the count of entity properties
via transitivity rules and (2) facilitating the transfer of entity
embeddings from two distinct KGs onto an identical space,
achieving 7.94% Hits@1 improvement over SOTA.

3.1 Symbolic representations of the knowledge
graph
Knowledge graphs (KGs) are represented as G = {E, R, F},
where E denotes the entity set, R represents the relation set,
and F constitutes the fact base. Each fact is expressed as
a triplet (es,r, eo), where es and eo denote the head and
tail entities, respectively, and r represents the relationship
between them. The size of the sets of entities and relations
are denoted as |E| = Ne and |R| = Nr.

To ﬁlter out possible noisy rules in the temp rules, we
adopt a relation performance-based noise ﬁltering method.
The core idea of this method is that both rules and embed-
dings model the overall data, and the correct triplets inferred
by them should be consistent. Therefore, if the performance
of a relation decreases after rule-generated triplets are added,
all the rules that use this relation as a rule head relation may
contain noise.
Two issues must be addressed: First, how can we deter-
mine whether the change in performance is due to the rules
or just training ﬂuctuations? Second, how can noise be accu-
rately identiﬁed while ensuring efﬁciency?
To address the ﬁrst issue, we run the baseline model mul-
tiple times to obtain the performance ﬂuctuation range for
each relation with a 99% conﬁdence interval. Speciﬁcally,
the average value and standard deviation are ﬁrst obtained
from multiple runs, and then 2.58 is used as the z value to
calculate the upper and lower bounds of the conﬁdence inter-
val. The upper bound of the performance for each relation is
expressed as M RRUpper, and the lower bound is expressed
as M RRLower. After adding the rule-generated triplets, the
performance of the relation is expressed as M RRrule. If
M RRrule > M RRUpper, the performance of that relation
is considered to have improved. If M RRrule < M RRLower,
the performance is considered to have worsened.
Although multiple runs effectively capture the perfor-
mance ﬂuctuation range for each relation, they signiﬁcantly
increase the framework’s runtime. To mitigate this runtime
increase, we adopt an optimized protocol, which is described
as follows:
1. Warm-start strategy: The baseline model ﬁrst trains
a certain number of rounds to establish a relatively sta-
ble initial point. Increasing the warm-up proportion reduces
both the total time needed to determine performance ﬂuctua-
tion ranges and the variance between relation performances
across runs. To balance training efﬁciency with obtaining
meaningful performance ranges, we set the warm-up phase
at 40% of the maximum training rounds in our experiment.
2. Resumed training: Subsequent runs reload this check-
point for continuation with the same training conﬁguration,
thus reducing the per-run training time.
Despite these optimizations, the total runtime remains
linearly proportional to the number of runs. This trade-off
between statistical reliability and computational efﬁciency

5.2 Evaluation task and metrics
The model evaluation employs the standard link prediction
task. For each test triplet (es, r, eo), either the head entity
es or the tail entity eo is replaced with every entity in the
entity set E to create candidate triplets. The model scores
these candidates and produces a ranked list, with evaluation
metrics calculated based on the true entities’ ranks.
Two standard evaluation metrics are used: mean reciprocal
rank (M RR) and the proportion of correct entities ranked in
the top N(Hit@N, N = 1, 3, 10). Higher values indicate
better performance.
When calculating evaluation metrics, the “ﬁlter” setting is
applied. It ignores scores of triplets that exist in the training,
validation, or testing set but are not the current test triplet.
This setting prevents correct entities from interfering with
the replaced entity.

6 Conclusion
In this work, we propose the NAAER model, in which a
score-based method for rule evaluation is employed and
potential noisy rules are fully taken into consideration. The
results of experiments conducted on both sparse datasets and
standard datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed
model. Our analysis demonstrates the wide applicability of
the score-based rule evaluation method and underscores the
importance of noise ﬁltering.
Currently, generating noisy rules involves evaluating mul-
tiple thresholds and ﬁltering them may overlook context-
depend noise. In future work, we aim to reﬁne these processes
to achieve efﬁcient operation with a single threshold, allow-
ing the model to leverage the advantages of rules while
maintaining efﬁciency. Additionally, given the proven poten-
tial of combining embedding and rule methods in previous
works, we will further explore the NAAER model’s appli-
cation capabilities in downstream tasks, such as question
answering, recommendation generation, and entity align-
ment.

Abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) is used to infer new facts from existing facts. Embedding-based KGC methods efﬁciently predict new facts by computing similarities among embeddings, whereas rule-based KGC methods achieve accuracy by applying logical rules. Both methods are combined in studies that involve evaluating rules on the basis of the matching degree between relation embeddings and scoring functions and using triplets derived from high-quality rules to enhance embedding learning. Despite notable improvements, these rule evaluation methods are limited to simple models, and potential noise in high-quality rules is frequently overlooked. To overcome these limitations, we propose the NAAER framework, a noise-aware and model-agnostic framework that iteratively reﬁnes embeddings and rules. Our key innovation lies in the implementation of a generalizable rule quality assessment that is conducted by measuring the absolute difference between the scores of the rule body and the head triplets, coupled with adaptive noise reduction that is achieved via performance-guided rule ﬁltering. Improvements in the link prediction performance of the NAAER framework were demonstrated using standard and sparse datasets, illustrating the broad applicability of the rule evaluation method.
